# ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ptr_meta/

## Expand description

A radioactive stabilization of the [ ptr_meta RFC](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2580-ptr-meta.html).

This crate provides the [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) trait,

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)

`from_raw_parts`[functions, and proc macros for deriving](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)

`to_raw_parts``Pointee` for
structs and implementing `Pointee` for trait objects.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Raw pointers can be decomposed into the data address and metadata components
with [ to_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)

`to_raw_parts_mut`Alternatively, metadata alone can be extracted with the [ metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
function. Although

[accepts pointers, references can be passed and will be implicitly coerced.](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)

`metadata`A pointer can be created from its address and metadata with
[ from_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)

`from_raw_parts_mut`[§](https://docs.rs#provided-impls)Provided impls

`ptr_meta` provides inherent implementations for many builtin types:

- All `Sized``Pointee`
- `slice`,- `str`, and- `CStr`
- `OsStr`(requires- `std`)
- `dyn Any`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`
- `dyn Error`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`

[§](https://docs.rs#structs-with-trailing-dsts)Structs with trailing DSTs

You can derive [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) for structs with trailing DSTs:

```
use ptr_meta::Pointee;
#[derive(Pointee)]
struct Block<H, T> {
    header: H,
    elements: [T],
}
```
Note that the last field is required to be a DST. Structs with a generic
type as the last field may have conflicting blanket implementations, as the
generic type may be `Sized`. A collection of specific implementations may be
required in these cases, with the generic parameter set (for example) a
slice, `str`, or specific trait object.

[§](https://docs.rs#trait-objects)Trait objects

You can generate [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) implementations for trait objects:

```
use ptr_meta::pointee;
// Generates Pointee for dyn Stringy
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Stringy {
    fn as_string(&self) -> String;
}
```
Note that this will not produce implementations for `Trait + Send + Sync`.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `derive`: Re-exports the macros from- `ptr_meta_derive`. Enabled by default.
- `std`: Enables additional impls for- `std`types. Enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Get the associated metadata for pointers
let str = "hello world";
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(str), str.len());
let slice = &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5] as &[i32];
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(slice), slice.len());
// Make your own wide pointers from data pointers and metadata
let bytes = [b'h', b'e', b'l', b'l', b'o'];
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<str>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
println!("{} world!", unsafe { &*ptr }); // prints "hello world!"
// Derive Pointee on your own types
#[derive(ptr_meta::Pointee)]
#[repr(transparent)]
struct CoolStr {
    inner: str,
}
impl CoolStr {
    fn print_cool(&self) {
        println!("😎 {} 😎", &self.inner);
    }
}
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<CoolStr>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
let cool = unsafe { &*ptr };
cool.print_cool(); // prints "😎 hello 😎"
// Implement Pointee for trait objects
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Printable {
    fn print(&self);
}
impl Printable for i32 {
    fn print(&self) {
        println!("i32: {self}");
    }
}
let i32_vtable = ptr_meta::metadata(&0i32 as &dyn Printable);
let one_hundred = 100i32;
let printable = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<dyn Printable>(
    (&one_hundred as *const i32).cast(),
    i32_vtable,
);
unsafe {
    (*printable).print(); // prints "i32: 100"
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [DynMetadata](https://docs.rs/struct.DynMetadata.html)
- The metadata for a trait object.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html)
- A trait which associates pointer metadata with a pointee type.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns a raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns a mutable raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
- Returns the metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns the data address and metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns the mutable data address and metadata of the given pointer.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [pointee](https://docs.rs/attr.pointee.html)- `derive`
- Generates a `Pointee`implementation for trait object of the labeled trait.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/derive.Pointee.html)- `derive`
- Derives `Pointee`for the labeled struct which has a trailing DST.

### derive (default)

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

---

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# synth_opt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/synth-opt/0.24.0/synth_opt/

## Expand description

Optimization passes for Synth compiler

This crate provides optimization passes that improve generated code quality.

[§](https://docs.rs#pass-types)Pass Types

- **Analysis Passes**: Gather information without modifying code
- **Transform Passes**: Modify code to improve quality
- **Cleanup Passes**: Remove dead/redundant code

[§](https://docs.rs#available-passes)Available Passes

- Dead Code Elimination (DCE)
- Constant Folding
- Common Subexpression Elimination (CSE)
- Loop-Invariant Code Motion (LICM)

# gravity_proto - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gravity_proto/0.11.0/gravity_proto/

## Expand description

This crate provides Gravity proto definitions in Rust and also re-exports cosmos_sdk_proto for use by downstream crates. By default around a dozen proto files are generated and places into the prost folder. We could then proceed to fix up all these files and use them as the required dependencies to the Gravity file, but we chose instead to replace those paths with references ot upstream cosmos-sdk-proto and delete the other files. This reduces cruft in this repo even if it does make for a somewhat more confusing proto generation process.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [cosmos_sdk_proto](https://docs.rs/cosmos-sdk-proto-althea/0.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cosmos_sdk_proto_althea/index.html);

- note to future readers I have hand copied the RegisteredInterchainAccount file from ibc.applications.interchain_accounts.v1.rs which is compiled but not checked in into gaia.icaauth.v1.rs

# synth_cfg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/synth-cfg/0.24.0/synth_cfg/

## Expand description

Control Flow Graph (CFG) for WebAssembly Functions

This crate provides CFG construction and analysis for WebAssembly functions, enabling proper branch target resolution and optimization.

[§](https://docs.rs#key-concepts)Key Concepts

- **Basic Block**: A maximal sequence of instructions with single entry and exit
- **CFG Edge**: Control flow from one basic block to another
- **Dominance**: Block A dominates B if all paths to B go through A
- **Loop**: A strongly connected component in the CFG

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Basic](https://docs.rs/struct.BasicBlock.html)- Block
- A basic block in the CFG
- [Cfg](https://docs.rs/struct.Cfg.html)
- Control Flow Graph
- [CfgBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.CfgBuilder.html)
- Builder for constructing CFGs
- [Loop](https://docs.rs/struct.Loop.html)
- Loop information

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [BlockId](https://docs.rs/type.BlockId.html)
- Block identifier

                # agnix

CLI for [agnix](https://github.com/agent-sh/agnix) - the agent configuration linter.

Validates agent configs across Claude Code, Codex/AGENTS.md, Cursor, Kiro, GitHub Copilot, and MCP.

```
## Usage

```
# Validate current directory
# Validate specific path
# Target specific tool
# Output as SARIF for CI integration
# Auto-fix issues
# Generate .agnix.toml schema
```
## Supported Configurations

- Agent skills (`SKILL.md`)
- Claude memory and instructions (`CLAUDE.md`,`CLAUDE.local.md`,`AGENTS.md`,`AGENTS.local.md`,`AGENTS.override.md`)
- Claude settings/hooks (`.claude/settings.json`,`.claude/settings.local.json`)

# agnix_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/agnix-core/0.37.0/agnix_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#agnix-core)agnix-core

Core validation engine for agent configurations.

Validates:

- Agent Skills (SKILL.md)
- Agent definitions (.md files with frontmatter)
- MCP tool configurations
- Claude Code hooks
- CLAUDE.md memory files
- Plugin manifests

This crate requires `std`. The `filesystem` Cargo feature (enabled by
default) adds file I/O dependencies; disabling it does not enable `no_std`.

[§](https://docs.rs#stability-tiers)Stability Tiers

Public modules are classified into stability tiers:

- **Stable**–- `config`,- `diagnostics`,- `fixes`,- `fs`. These modules follow semver: breaking changes require a major version bump.
- **Unstable**–- `authoring`,- `eval`,- `i18n`,- `validation`. Interfaces may change on minor releases. Use with care in downstream crates.
- **Internal**–- `parsers`(pub(crate)). Not part of the public API. Some types are re-exported at the crate root with- `#[doc(hidden)]`for fuzz/bench/test use only.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- Registry that maps `FileType`
- [Validator](https://docs.rs/struct.ValidatorRegistryBuilder.html)- Registry - Builder
- Builder for constructing a `ValidatorRegistry`

# agnix_rules - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/agnix-rules/0.37.0/agnix_rules/

## Expand description

Validation rules for agnix - agent configuration linter.

This crate provides the rule definitions used by agnix to validate agent configurations including Skills, Hooks, MCP servers, Memory files, and Plugins.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

```
use agnix_rules::{RULES_DATA, RULES_METADATA, VALID_TOOLS, TOOL_RULE_PREFIXES};
// RULES_DATA is a static array of (rule_id, rule_name) tuples
for (id, name) in RULES_DATA {
    println!("{}: {}", id, name);
}
// VALID_TOOLS contains all tool names from rules.json
for tool in VALID_TOOLS {
    println!("Tool: {}", tool);
}
// TOOL_RULE_PREFIXES maps rule prefixes to their tools
for (prefix, tool) in TOOL_RULE_PREFIXES {
    println!("Prefix {} -> Tool {}", prefix, tool);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rule-categories)Rule Categories

- **AS-xxx**: Agent Skills
- **CC-xxx**: Claude Code (Hooks, Skills, Memory, etc.)
- **MCP-xxx**: Model Context Protocol
- **COP-xxx**: GitHub Copilot
- **CUR-xxx**: Cursor
- **XML-xxx**: XML/XSLT based configs
- **XP-xxx**: Cross-platform rules

- [AUTHORING_](https://docs.rs/constant.AUTHORING_CATALOG_JSON.html)- CATALOG_ - JSON
- Raw authoring catalog JSON (top-level `authoring`section from rules.json). This is generated at build time to keep rules.json as the source of truth.
- [AUTHORING_](https://docs.rs/constant.AUTHORING_FAMILIES.html)- FAMILIES
- Authoring family IDs derived from rules.json authoring.families.
- [AUTHORING_](https://docs.rs/constant.AUTHORING_VERSION.html)- VERSION
- Authoring catalog schema version.
- [RULES_](https://docs.rs/constant.RULES_DATA.html)- DATA
- Rule data as (id, name) tuples.
- [RULES_](https://docs.rs/constant.RULES_METADATA.html)- METADATA
- Rule metadata as (id, category, severity, tool) tuples.
- [TOOL_](https://docs.rs/constant.TOOL_RULE_PREFIXES.html)- RULE_ - PREFIXES
- Mapping of rule ID prefixes to their associated tools.
- [VALID_](https://docs.rs/constant.VALID_TOOLS.html)- TOOLS
- Valid tool names derived from rules.json evidence.applies_to.tool.

# kigumi_test - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kigumi-test/0.1.0/kigumi_test/

## Expand description

Integration-test kit: a FAST, correct database reset plus the fixtures every test used to copy-paste (the DATABASE_URL skip, the superuser Ctx, the insert helper).

The reset is fingerprinted. A full drop/create of the whole migration plan costs ~minutes per
binary; most runs don’t change the schema at all. So [ TestDb::new](https://docs.rs/struct.TestDb.html#method.new):

- takes a global advisory lock on a DEDICATED connection (concurrent test binaries sharing one DATABASE_URL serialize instead of clobbering each other; the lock lives until the connection drops at the end of the test),
- computes a CODE fingerprint (the DDL projection of every registered model + the M2M junction
shapes + `KIT_SCHEMA_VERSION`
- if both match what the last full build recorded → `TRUNCATE <everything> RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE`(milliseconds) and re-run the idempotent`ensure_*`framework DDL (an additive framework change self-applies here and the stored snapshot is refreshed),
- otherwise → full drop/create of every table in the schema, then record the new fingerprints.

The DB snapshot check also catches schema “dirt” left by DDL-exercising tests (e.g. runtime
custom fields ALTERing a table): the snapshot no longer matches, so the next reset rebuilds.
Residual manual knob: a DESTRUCTIVE change to framework `ensure_*` DDL (a column retyped in
place — additive `IF NOT EXISTS` changes self-apply) needs a [ KIT_SCHEMA_VERSION](https://docs.rs/constant.KIT_SCHEMA_VERSION.html) bump.

The fingerprint is per test BINARY (it hashes the models linked into it): binaries linking different module sets still rebuild when they alternate — the win is the dev loop (re-running one binary) and consecutive binaries sharing a module set.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [TestDb](https://docs.rs/struct.TestDb.html)
- A connected, reset test database. Holds the advisory lock for the lifetime of the value — drop it (end of test) and the dedicated lock connection closes, releasing the lock server-side.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [KIT_](https://docs.rs/constant.KIT_SCHEMA_VERSION.html)- SCHEMA_ - VERSION
- Bump when a framework DDL change guarded by `IF NOT EXISTS`cannot self-apply on the TRUNCATE path (destructive shape changes to`ensure_*`tables; junction-template changes are fingerprinted verbatim via`m2m_junction_ddl`and self-detect). Additive`CREATE/ADD ... IF NOT EXISTS`changes do not need a bump.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [ins](https://docs.rs/fn.ins.html)
- The shared insert fixture (the `ins`closure every test used to define): a secured insert as`ctx`with no ACL/rule overlays, unwrapped. Panics on failure — it’s a fixture, not the subject.
- [prepare](https://docs.rs/fn.prepare.html)
- Resets the database for this binary’s registered model set (see the module doc for the
fingerprint strategy). Public so a bespoke harness can drive it without `TestDb``TestDb::new`
- [su](https://docs.rs/fn.su.html)
- The superuser context every test seeds with.

# harn_rules_hostlib - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/harn-rules-hostlib/0.8.168/harn_rules_hostlib/

## Expand description

Host capability exposing the `harn-rules` declarative rule engine to
Harn as `rules.search` / `rules.report` / `rules.apply`.

This crate lives outside `harn-hostlib` on purpose: `harn-rules` already
depends on `harn-hostlib` (for the tree-sitter grammars), so the rules
builtins would form a dependency cycle if they lived there. An embedder
(harn-cli, harn-serve) calls [ install](https://docs.rs/fn.install.html) alongside

`harn_hostlib::install_default`.[§](https://docs.rs#builtins)Builtins

- `rules.search`(read-only) — run a rule and return its matches.
- `rules.report`(read-only) — run a rule in report-only mode and return a- `harn_rules::DataTable`
- `rules.diagnostics`(read-only) — run a- **declarative**rule and return its- `harn_rules::Diagnostic`
- `rules.visit`(read-only,- **async**) — the- **imperative**escape hatch: run a rule’s matcher, then invoke a- `.harn`visitor- `on_match($node, $ctx)`once per match. The visitor returns its report(s) —- `nil`/- `false`to skip, a- `{message, fix, safety}`dict, or a list of them — which the engine turns into diagnostics of the same shape- `rules.diagnostics`emits. The visitor has full programmatic control (compute a message/fix from the captured metavars), which the declarative form cannot.
- `rules.apply`(write-gated) — apply a codemod rule’s- `fix`; writes only when- `dry_run: false`- *and*the rule is safe to auto-apply (or- `allow_unsafe: true`). Shares the deterministic-tools gate with the other mutating builtins.

A rule is passed as its TOML source (`rule`), so an agent can author and
run a rule — declarative *or* imperative — entirely from `.harn` without
recompiling the binary.

[§](https://docs.rs#why-rulesvisit-is-async-and-why-it-returns-rather-than-mutates)Why `rules.visit` is async, and why it returns rather than mutates

A *synchronous* hostlib builtin cannot call a `.harn` closure: the VM’s
[ Vm::call_closure_pub](https://docs.rs/harn-vm/0.8.168/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/harn_vm/vm/state/struct.Vm.html#method.call_closure_pub) is async-only. So the visitor is registered as an

**async**builtin (directly on the VM via

[, bypassing the sync](https://docs.rs/harn-vm/0.8.168/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/harn_vm/vm/state/struct.Vm.html#method.register_async_builtin)

`Vm::register_async_builtin`[), which can obtain a child VM from its](https://docs.rs/harn-hostlib/0.8.168/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/harn_hostlib/registry/struct.HostlibRegistry.html)

`HostlibRegistry`[and call back per match.](https://docs.rs/harn-vm/0.8.168/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/harn_vm/vm/async_builtin/struct.AsyncBuiltinCtx.html)

`AsyncBuiltinCtx`The visitor **returns** its reports instead of calling a mutating
`ctx.report(...)`: Harn closures capture by value, so a Harn-side
accumulator could not collect across calls, and `VmValue` has no callable
variant that carries captured Rust state to embed a stateful `report`
method in `ctx`. Returning is both the sound option and the simpler one.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Lint](https://docs.rs/struct.LintCapability.html)- Capability
- The `lint`host capability (#2851): runs the Harn linter for an agent/IDE/cloud caller, returning the same diagnostics the CLI emits.
- [Rules](https://docs.rs/struct.RulesCapability.html)- Capability
- The `rules`host capability.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [install](https://docs.rs/fn.install.html)
- Install the `rules`+`lint`capabilities into a VM. Call this alongside`harn_hostlib::install_default`.

# bitlist - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bitlist/0.0.5/bitlist/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#bitlist)bitlist

Word-sized bit list implementation with bigint functionality.

Main type of this crate is `BitList` - dynamic bitset storing up to 57 bits (on 64-bit target) inline without allocation, heap allocating for more bits.

Size of `BitList` is equal to `size_of::<usize>()`, type is also niche optmizated so `Option<BitList>` is same size as `BitList`.

The crate is under developement, it’s missing documentation and examples. But is otherwise usefull and most of the methods do what you expect. Please also checkout `BitsIter` type as it is not only an iterator but also has methods to effeciently find bits in sparse lists.

# perfectstar2k 0.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/perfectstar2k/0.2.0

# PerfectStar 2k

A modern TUI homage to **WordStar for DOS** and **WordPerfect 5.1** — a real
daily-driver writing tool, inspired by Robert J. Sawyer's essay
[ A Writer's Word Processor](https://www.sfwriter.com/wordstar.htm).

Plain text and Markdown in, prose out. WordStar's touch-typist command language and "long-hand page" metaphor; WordPerfect's clean blue screen and Reveal Codes; a few of Emacs's best ideas (kill ring, incremental search, never-lose undo) folded in where they serve a writer.

```
cargo run --release -- draft.md
```
## The philosophy

- **Hands never leave the home row.**Every command is a Ctrl chord with a positional mnemonic. Arrow keys, PgUp/PgDn, Home/End also work — WordStar itself allowed the same.
- **The long-hand page.**Mark a block now, decide what to do with it hours later. Ten bookmarks. A jump ring that remembers where you were. Notes to yourself (- `..`lines) that display dimmed and never export.
- **Least modal.**Writing and editing are one continuum. No modes to enter, no menus to descend for common operations.
- **The tool adapts to the writer.**Config for theme, menu delay, autosave, wrap margin, and help levels from hand-holding to a completely clean screen.

## Keys

The diamond (with `^Q…` prefix chords, press the second key plain or with Ctrl):

| `^E ^S ^D ^X` | cursor diamond | `^A ^F` | word left / right |
| `^W ^Z` | scroll line | `^R ^C` | page up / down |
| `^QS ^QD` | line start / end | `^QE ^QX` | screen top / bottom |
| `^QR ^QC` | document top / bottom | `^Q, ^Q.` | sentence back / forward |
| `^Q[ ^Q]` | paragraph back / forward | `^QP` | previous position (walks the ring) |
| `^QO` | outline: jump between Markdown headings | `^QN` | next misspelled word |

Editing:

| `^G`/`^H` | delete char / left | `^T` | delete word |
| `^Y` | delete line | `^QY` | delete to line end |
| `^U` | undo (never loses a state; redo = undo an undo) | `^N` | open line |
| `^QT`/`^QG` | transpose words / chars | `^V` | insert / overtype |
| `^QM` | record macro | `^QJ` | play macro |

Blocks, bookmarks, and the kill ring:

| `^KB ^KK` | mark block begin / end — whenever you like | `^KC ^KV` | copy / move block to cursor |
| `^KY` | delete block | `^KH` | hide/show highlight |
| `^KU` | toggle previous block | `^KW ^KR` | write block / read file |
| `^KP` | put a clipping; press again to cycle older ones | `^QB ^QK ^QV` | jump to block begin / end / source |
| `^K0–9` | set bookmark | `^Q0–9` | jump to bookmark |

Search, files, screen:

| `^QF` | incremental search | `^L` | find next |
| `^QA` | find & replace (g/n/w options) | `Esc`/`F1` | command palette |
| `^KD ^KS` | save (atomic, with one-time `.bak`) | `^KX` | save & exit |
| `^KQ` | quit | `^KE` | export with `..`notes stripped |
| `^KM` | export standard-manuscript-format RTF | `^OD` | Reveal Codes |
| `^OB` | cycle theme | `^OW ^OR` | word wrap / wrap margin |
| `^OH` | help level (0 clean · 1 menus · 2 hints) | `^OT` | typewriter scrolling on/off |
| `^OS` | spellcheck on/off | `^OA` | add word under cursor to personal dictionary |

Hold any prefix (`^K` `^Q` `^O`) briefly and its menu appears, WordStar style.

## Sessions

Cursor position, bookmarks, block marks, the jump ring, and full undo history persist per file (under the user data dir — your manuscript's folder stays clean). Reopen a draft and your fingers are still in the pages.

## Spellcheck

A bundled Hunspell-compatible en_US dictionary (via
[ spellbook](https://crates.io/crates/spellbook)) underlines misspelled
words on the fly — no network, no system dictionary required.

`^QN` jumps to
the next one; `^OA` adds the word under the cursor to a personal dictionary
that's global across every document (essential for character names and
invented words) and persists at
`~/.config/perfectstar2k/personal_dict.txt`. See
[THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md](https://docs.rs/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md)for the dictionary's attribution.

## Manuscript export

`^KM` writes a **standard-manuscript-format RTF** — the layout agents and
editors expect for fiction submissions: 12pt serif, double-spaced, 1-inch
margins, first-line-indented paragraphs, chapters (`#` headings) starting on
a fresh page, `*italic*`/`**bold**` rendered as real emphasis (not literal
asterisks), and straight quotes/dashes upgraded to typographic ones. `..`
note lines are stripped, same as `^KE`. It's hand-generated RTF — no
dependencies, no external converter. (`^KE` still exists for a plain-text
copy with notes stripped.)

## Config

`~/.config/perfectstar2k/config.toml`:

```
 = "wp-blue"        # wp-blue | wordstar | terminal
 = 700
 = 60       # 0 disables
 = true
 = 0          # 0 = window width
 = 1           # 0 clean · 1 delayed menus · 2 menus + hint bar
 = true
 = false       # pin the current line, scroll the page under it
 = "times"  # times | courier — for ^KM RTF export
```
## Build

Rust 2024. `cargo build --release` produces the `pstar` binary.
`cargo test` runs the buffer/undo/wrap/markdown/rtf unit suites.

# ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ptr_meta/0.3.1/target-redirect/ptr_meta/

## Expand description

A radioactive stabilization of the [ ptr_meta RFC](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2580-ptr-meta.html).

This crate provides the [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) trait,

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)

`from_raw_parts`[functions, and proc macros for deriving](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)

`to_raw_parts``Pointee` for
structs and implementing `Pointee` for trait objects.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Raw pointers can be decomposed into the data address and metadata components
with [ to_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)

`to_raw_parts_mut`Alternatively, metadata alone can be extracted with the [ metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
function. Although

[accepts pointers, references can be passed and will be implicitly coerced.](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)

`metadata`A pointer can be created from its address and metadata with
[ from_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)

`from_raw_parts_mut`[§](https://docs.rs#provided-impls)Provided impls

`ptr_meta` provides inherent implementations for many builtin types:

- All `Sized``Pointee`
- `slice`,- `str`, and- `CStr`
- `OsStr`(requires- `std`)
- `dyn Any`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`
- `dyn Error`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`

[§](https://docs.rs#structs-with-trailing-dsts)Structs with trailing DSTs

You can derive [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) for structs with trailing DSTs:

```
use ptr_meta::Pointee;
#[derive(Pointee)]
struct Block<H, T> {
    header: H,
    elements: [T],
}
```
Note that the last field is required to be a DST. Structs with a generic
type as the last field may have conflicting blanket implementations, as the
generic type may be `Sized`. A collection of specific implementations may be
required in these cases, with the generic parameter set (for example) a
slice, `str`, or specific trait object.

[§](https://docs.rs#trait-objects)Trait objects

You can generate [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) implementations for trait objects:

```
use ptr_meta::pointee;
// Generates Pointee for dyn Stringy
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Stringy {
    fn as_string(&self) -> String;
}
```
Note that this will not produce implementations for `Trait + Send + Sync`.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `derive`: Re-exports the macros from- `ptr_meta_derive`. Enabled by default.
- `std`: Enables additional impls for- `std`types. Enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Get the associated metadata for pointers
let str = "hello world";
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(str), str.len());
let slice = &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5] as &[i32];
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(slice), slice.len());
// Make your own wide pointers from data pointers and metadata
let bytes = [b'h', b'e', b'l', b'l', b'o'];
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<str>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
println!("{} world!", unsafe { &*ptr }); // prints "hello world!"
// Derive Pointee on your own types
#[derive(ptr_meta::Pointee)]
#[repr(transparent)]
struct CoolStr {
    inner: str,
}
impl CoolStr {
    fn print_cool(&self) {
        println!("😎 {} 😎", &self.inner);
    }
}
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<CoolStr>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
let cool = unsafe { &*ptr };
cool.print_cool(); // prints "😎 hello 😎"
// Implement Pointee for trait objects
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Printable {
    fn print(&self);
}
impl Printable for i32 {
    fn print(&self) {
        println!("i32: {self}");
    }
}
let i32_vtable = ptr_meta::metadata(&0i32 as &dyn Printable);
let one_hundred = 100i32;
let printable = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<dyn Printable>(
    (&one_hundred as *const i32).cast(),
    i32_vtable,
);
unsafe {
    (*printable).print(); // prints "i32: 100"
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [DynMetadata](https://docs.rs/struct.DynMetadata.html)
- The metadata for a trait object.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html)
- A trait which associates pointer metadata with a pointee type.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns a raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns a mutable raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
- Returns the metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns the data address and metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns the mutable data address and metadata of the given pointer.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [pointee](https://docs.rs/attr.pointee.html)- `derive`
- Generates a `Pointee`implementation for trait object of the labeled trait.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/derive.Pointee.html)- `derive`
- Derives `Pointee`for the labeled struct which has a trailing DST.

# ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ptr_meta/0.3.1/ptr_meta/index.html

## Expand description

A radioactive stabilization of the [ ptr_meta RFC](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2580-ptr-meta.html).

This crate provides the [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) trait,

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)

`from_raw_parts`[functions, and proc macros for deriving](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)

`to_raw_parts``Pointee` for
structs and implementing `Pointee` for trait objects.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Raw pointers can be decomposed into the data address and metadata components
with [ to_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)

`to_raw_parts_mut`Alternatively, metadata alone can be extracted with the [ metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
function. Although

[accepts pointers, references can be passed and will be implicitly coerced.](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)

`metadata`A pointer can be created from its address and metadata with
[ from_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)

`from_raw_parts_mut`[§](https://docs.rs#provided-impls)Provided impls

`ptr_meta` provides inherent implementations for many builtin types:

- All `Sized``Pointee`
- `slice`,- `str`, and- `CStr`
- `OsStr`(requires- `std`)
- `dyn Any`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`
- `dyn Error`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`

[§](https://docs.rs#structs-with-trailing-dsts)Structs with trailing DSTs

You can derive [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) for structs with trailing DSTs:

```
use ptr_meta::Pointee;
#[derive(Pointee)]
struct Block<H, T> {
    header: H,
    elements: [T],
}
```
Note that the last field is required to be a DST. Structs with a generic
type as the last field may have conflicting blanket implementations, as the
generic type may be `Sized`. A collection of specific implementations may be
required in these cases, with the generic parameter set (for example) a
slice, `str`, or specific trait object.

[§](https://docs.rs#trait-objects)Trait objects

You can generate [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) implementations for trait objects:

```
use ptr_meta::pointee;
// Generates Pointee for dyn Stringy
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Stringy {
    fn as_string(&self) -> String;
}
```
Note that this will not produce implementations for `Trait + Send + Sync`.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `derive`: Re-exports the macros from- `ptr_meta_derive`. Enabled by default.
- `std`: Enables additional impls for- `std`types. Enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Get the associated metadata for pointers
let str = "hello world";
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(str), str.len());
let slice = &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5] as &[i32];
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(slice), slice.len());
// Make your own wide pointers from data pointers and metadata
let bytes = [b'h', b'e', b'l', b'l', b'o'];
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<str>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
println!("{} world!", unsafe { &*ptr }); // prints "hello world!"
// Derive Pointee on your own types
#[derive(ptr_meta::Pointee)]
#[repr(transparent)]
struct CoolStr {
    inner: str,
}
impl CoolStr {
    fn print_cool(&self) {
        println!("😎 {} 😎", &self.inner);
    }
}
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<CoolStr>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
let cool = unsafe { &*ptr };
cool.print_cool(); // prints "😎 hello 😎"
// Implement Pointee for trait objects
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Printable {
    fn print(&self);
}
impl Printable for i32 {
    fn print(&self) {
        println!("i32: {self}");
    }
}
let i32_vtable = ptr_meta::metadata(&0i32 as &dyn Printable);
let one_hundred = 100i32;
let printable = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<dyn Printable>(
    (&one_hundred as *const i32).cast(),
    i32_vtable,
);
unsafe {
    (*printable).print(); // prints "i32: 100"
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- The metadata for a trait object.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns a mutable raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
- Returns the metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns the data address and metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns the mutable data address and metadata of the given pointer.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! A radioactive stabilization of the [`ptr_meta` RFC][rfc].
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!

[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! [`to_raw_parts`] functions, and proc macros for deriving `Pointee` for

[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!

[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! with [`to_raw_parts`] or [`to_raw_parts_mut`].
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! Alternatively, metadata alone can be extracted with the [`metadata`]
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! function. Although [`metadata`] accepts pointers, references can be passed

[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! A pointer can be created from its address and metadata with

[102](https://docs.rs#102)
[103](https://docs.rs#103)/// A trait which associates pointer metadata with a pointee type.
[104](https://docs.rs#104)///
[105](https://docs.rs#105)/// # Pointer metadata
[106](https://docs.rs#106)///
[107](https://docs.rs#107)/// Pointers and references can be thought of as having two parts: a data
[108](https://docs.rs#108)/// address and some extra "pointer metadata".
[109](https://docs.rs#109)///
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// Pointers to [statically-sized types](`Sized`) and `extern` types are
[111](https://docs.rs#111)/// "narrow": their pointer metadata is `()`.
[112](https://docs.rs#112)///
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// Pointers to [dynamically-sized types][dst] are "wide": they have pointer
[114](https://docs.rs#114)/// metadata with a non-zero size. There are four classes of dynamically-sized
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// types currently available:
[116](https://docs.rs#116)///
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// * `str`s have `usize` pointer metadata equal to the length of the string
[118](https://docs.rs#118)///   slice in bytes.
[119](https://docs.rs#119)/// * Slices like `[i32]` have `usize` pointer metadata equal to the length of
[120](https://docs.rs#120)///   the slice in items.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)/// * Trait objects like `dyn SomeTrait` have [`DynMetadata`] pointer metadata,
[122](https://docs.rs#122)///   which point to the trait objects' virtual method tables.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)/// * Structs with a trailing DST have the same metadata as the trailing DST.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)///
[125](https://docs.rs#125)/// In the future, Rust may add new kinds of types which have different pointer
[126](https://docs.rs#126)/// metadata.
[127](https://docs.rs#127)///
[128](https://docs.rs#128)/// [dst]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/dynamically-sized-types.html
[129](https://docs.rs#129)///
[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// # Safety
[131](https://docs.rs#131)///
[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// The associated `Metadata` type must be the pointer metadata type for the
[133](https://docs.rs#133)/// implementing type.
[134](https://docs.rs#134)pub unsafe trait Pointee {
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    /// The metadata type for pointers and references to this type.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)    type Metadata: Copy + Send + Sync + Ord + Hash + Unpin;
[137](https://docs.rs#137)}
[138](https://docs.rs#138)
[139](https://docs.rs#139)// SAFETY: Pointers to `Sized` types have no metadata (i.e. their metadata is
[140](https://docs.rs#140)// the unit type `()`).
[141](https://docs.rs#141)unsafe impl<T> Pointee for T {
[142](https://docs.rs#142)    type Metadata = ();
[143](https://docs.rs#143)}
[144](https://docs.rs#144)
[145](https://docs.rs#145)// SAFETY: Pointers to slices have a `usize` representing the length of the
[146](https://docs.rs#146)// slice in elements as their metadata.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)unsafe impl<T> Pointee for [T] {
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    type Metadata = usize;
[149](https://docs.rs#149)}
[150](https://docs.rs#150)
[151](https://docs.rs#151)// SAFETY: String slice pointers have a `usize` representing the length of the
[152](https://docs.rs#152)// string slice in bytes as their metadata.
[153](https://docs.rs#153)unsafe impl Pointee for str {
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    type Metadata = usize;
[155](https://docs.rs#155)}
[156](https://docs.rs#156)
[157](https://docs.rs#157)// SAFETY: `CStr` pointers have a `usize` representing the length of the
[158](https://docs.rs#158)// C-string slice in bytes (nul included) as their metadata.
[159](https://docs.rs#159)unsafe impl Pointee for CStr {
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    type Metadata = usize;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)}
[162](https://docs.rs#162)
[163](https://docs.rs#163)#[cfg(feature = "std")]
[164](https://docs.rs#164)// SAFETY: `OsStr` pointers have a `usize` representing the length of the
[165](https://docs.rs#165)// string in bytes as their metadata.
[166](https://docs.rs#166)unsafe impl Pointee for std::ffi::OsStr {
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    type Metadata = usize;
[168](https://docs.rs#168)}
[169](https://docs.rs#169)
[170](https://docs.rs#170)/// Returns the metadata of the given pointer.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)///
[172](https://docs.rs#172)/// `*mut T`, `&T`, and `&mut T` can all be passed directly to this function as
[173](https://docs.rs#173)/// they implicitly coerce to `*const T`.
[174](https://docs.rs#174)///
[175](https://docs.rs#175)/// # Example
[176](https://docs.rs#176)///
[177](https://docs.rs#177)/// ```
[178](https://docs.rs#178)/// // String slices have pointer metadata equal to their size in bytes
[179](https://docs.rs#179)/// assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata("foo"), 3_usize);
[180](https://docs.rs#180)/// ```
[181](https://docs.rs#181)#[inline]
[182](https://docs.rs#182)pub const fn metadata<T: Pointee + ?Sized>(
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    ptr: *const T,
[184](https://docs.rs#184)) -> <T as Pointee>::Metadata {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    // SAFETY: Accessing the value from the `PtrRepr` union is safe since
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    // *const T and PtrComponents<T> have the same memory layouts. Only std can
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    // make this guarantee.
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    unsafe { PtrRepr { const_ptr: ptr }.components.metadata }
[189](https://docs.rs#189)}
[190](https://docs.rs#190)
[191](https://docs.rs#191)/// Returns the data address and metadata of the given pointer.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)///
[193](https://docs.rs#193)/// `*mut T`, `&T`, and `&mut T` can all be passed directly to this function as
[194](https://docs.rs#194)/// they implicitly coerce to `*const T`.
[195](https://docs.rs#195)///
[196](https://docs.rs#196)/// # Example
[197](https://docs.rs#197)///
[198](https://docs.rs#198)/// ```
[199](https://docs.rs#199)/// let (data_address, metadata) = ptr_meta::to_raw_parts("foo");
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// assert_ne!(data_address, core::ptr::null());
[201](https://docs.rs#201)/// assert_eq!(metadata, 3);
[202](https://docs.rs#202)/// ```
[203](https://docs.rs#203)#[inline]
[204](https://docs.rs#204)pub const fn to_raw_parts<T: Pointee + ?Sized>(
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    ptr: *const T,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)) -> (*const (), <T as Pointee>::Metadata) {
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    (ptr as *const (), metadata(ptr))
[208](https://docs.rs#208)}
[209](https://docs.rs#209)
[210](https://docs.rs#210)/// Returns the mutable data address and metadata of the given pointer.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)///
[212](https://docs.rs#212)/// See [`to_raw_parts`] for more details.
[213](https://docs.rs#213)#[inline]
[214](https://docs.rs#214)pub const fn to_raw_parts_mut<T: Pointee + ?Sized>(
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    ptr: *mut T,
[216](https://docs.rs#216)) -> (*mut (), <T as Pointee>::Metadata) {
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    (ptr as *mut (), metadata(ptr))
[218](https://docs.rs#218)}
[219](https://docs.rs#219)
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// Returns a raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
[221](https://docs.rs#221)///
[222](https://docs.rs#222)/// This function is safe, but the returned pointer is not necessarily safe to
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// dereference. For slices, see the documentation of [`slice::from_raw_parts`]
[224](https://docs.rs#224)/// for safety requirements. For trait objects, the metadata must come from a
[225](https://docs.rs#225)/// a trait object with the same underlying type.
[226](https://docs.rs#226)///
[227](https://docs.rs#227)/// [`slice::from_raw_parts`]: core::slice::from_raw_parts
[228](https://docs.rs#228)#[inline]
[229](https://docs.rs#229)pub const fn from_raw_parts<T: Pointee + ?Sized>(
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    data_address: *const (),
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    metadata: <T as Pointee>::Metadata,
[232](https://docs.rs#232)) -> *const T {
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    // SAFETY: Accessing the value from the `PtrRepr` union is safe since
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    // *const T and PtrComponents<T> have the same memory layouts. Only std can
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    // make this guarantee.
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    unsafe {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        PtrRepr {
[238](https://docs.rs#238)            components: PtrComponents {
[239](https://docs.rs#239)                data_address,
[240](https://docs.rs#240)                metadata,
[241](https://docs.rs#241)            },
[242](https://docs.rs#242)        }
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        .const_ptr
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)}
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// Returns a mutable raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)///
[249](https://docs.rs#249)/// See [`from_raw_parts`] for more details.
[250](https://docs.rs#250)#[inline]
[251](https://docs.rs#251)pub const fn from_raw_parts_mut<T: Pointee + ?Sized>(
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    data_address: *mut (),
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    metadata: <T as Pointee>::Metadata,
[254](https://docs.rs#254)) -> *mut T {
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    // SAFETY: Accessing the value from the `PtrRepr` union is safe since
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    // *const T and PtrComponents<T> have the same memory layouts. Only std can
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    // make this guarantee.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    unsafe {
[259](https://docs.rs#259)        PtrRepr {
[260](https://docs.rs#260)            components: PtrComponents {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)                data_address,
[262](https://docs.rs#262)                metadata,
[263](https://docs.rs#263)            },
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        }
[265](https://docs.rs#265)        .mut_ptr
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    }
[267](https://docs.rs#267)}
[268](https://docs.rs#268)
[269](https://docs.rs#269)#[repr(C)]
[270](https://docs.rs#270)union PtrRepr<T: Pointee + ?Sized> {
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    const_ptr: *const T,
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    mut_ptr: *mut T,
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    components: PtrComponents<T>,
[274](https://docs.rs#274)}

[292](https://docs.rs#292)/// The metadata for a trait object.
[293](https://docs.rs#293)///
[294](https://docs.rs#294)/// This struct wraps a pointer to a vtable (virtual method table) which
[295](https://docs.rs#295)/// contains all of the necessary information to manipulate the concrete type
[296](https://docs.rs#296)/// stored inside of the trait object:
[297](https://docs.rs#297)///
[298](https://docs.rs#298)/// * The size and alignment of the concrete type
[299](https://docs.rs#299)/// * A function pointer to the type's `drop_in_place` impl
[300](https://docs.rs#300)/// * Function pointers for each method in the concrete type's trait
[301](https://docs.rs#301)///   implementation
[302](https://docs.rs#302)///
[303](https://docs.rs#303)/// Providing a type argument that is not a `dyn` trait object is possible, but
[304](https://docs.rs#304)/// does not correspond with a meaningful type.
[305](https://docs.rs#305)pub struct DynMetadata<Dyn: ?Sized> {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    vtable_ptr: &'static VTable,
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<Dyn>,
[308](https://docs.rs#308)}
[309](https://docs.rs#309)
[310](https://docs.rs#310)// Extern types are not stable, so we substitute a ZST. This is not a perfect
[311](https://docs.rs#311)// substitute but it's not exposed anywhere so it's close enough.
[312](https://docs.rs#312)struct VTable;
[313](https://docs.rs#313)
[314](https://docs.rs#314)impl<Dyn: ?Sized> DynMetadata<Dyn> {
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    /// Returns the size of the type associated with this metadata.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    #[inline]
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    pub fn size_of(self) -> usize {
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        #[cfg(miri)]
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        {
[320](https://docs.rs#320)            // Note that "size stored in vtable" is *not* the same as "result of
[321](https://docs.rs#321)            // size_of_val_raw". Consider a reference like `&(i32,
[322](https://docs.rs#322)            // dyn Send)`: the vtable will only store the size of the
[323](https://docs.rs#323)            // `Send` part!
[324](https://docs.rs#324)            // SAFETY: DynMetadata always contains a valid vtable pointer
[325](https://docs.rs#325)            return unsafe {
[326](https://docs.rs#326)                core::intrinsics::vtable_size(
[327](https://docs.rs#327)                    self.vtable_ptr as *const VTable as *const (),
[328](https://docs.rs#328)                )
[329](https://docs.rs#329)            };
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        }
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        #[cfg(not(miri))]
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)            // SAFETY: This happens to be true. It may not always be true. The
[334](https://docs.rs#334)            // location of the size for vtables is based on the implementation
[335](https://docs.rs#335)            // of the vtable_size intrinsic.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)            unsafe {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)                (self.vtable_ptr as *const VTable as *const usize)
[338](https://docs.rs#338)                    .add(1)
[339](https://docs.rs#339)                    .read()
[340](https://docs.rs#340)            }
[341](https://docs.rs#341)        }
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    }
[343](https://docs.rs#343)
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    /// Returns the alignment of the type associated with this metadata.
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    #[inline]
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    pub fn align_of(self) -> usize {
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        #[cfg(miri)]
[348](https://docs.rs#348)        {
[349](https://docs.rs#349)            // SAFETY: DynMetadata always contains a valid vtable pointer
[350](https://docs.rs#350)            return unsafe {
[351](https://docs.rs#351)                core::intrinsics::vtable_align(
[352](https://docs.rs#352)                    self.vtable_ptr as *const VTable as *const (),
[353](https://docs.rs#353)                )
[354](https://docs.rs#354)            };
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        }
[356](https://docs.rs#356)        #[cfg(not(miri))]
[357](https://docs.rs#357)        {
[358](https://docs.rs#358)            // SAFETY: This happens to be true. It may not always be true. The
[359](https://docs.rs#359)            // location of the alignment for vtables is based on the
[360](https://docs.rs#360)            // implementation of the vtable_align intrinsic.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)            unsafe {
[362](https://docs.rs#362)                (self.vtable_ptr as *const VTable as *const usize)
[363](https://docs.rs#363)                    .add(2)
[364](https://docs.rs#364)                    .read()
[365](https://docs.rs#365)            }
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        }
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    }
[368](https://docs.rs#368)
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// Returns the layout of the type associated with this metadata.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    #[inline]
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    pub fn layout(self) -> core::alloc::Layout {
[372](https://docs.rs#372)        // SAFETY: the compiler emitted this vtable for a concrete Rust type
[373](https://docs.rs#373)        // which is known to have a valid layout. Same rationale as in
[374](https://docs.rs#374)        // `Layout::for_value`.
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        unsafe {
[376](https://docs.rs#376)            core::alloc::Layout::from_size_align_unchecked(
[377](https://docs.rs#377)                self.size_of(),
[378](https://docs.rs#378)                self.align_of(),
[379](https://docs.rs#379)            )
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        }
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    }
[382](https://docs.rs#382)}

# Pointee in ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ptr_meta/0.3.1/ptr_meta/trait.Pointee.html

## Expand description

A trait which associates pointer metadata with a pointee type.

[§](https://docs.rs#pointer-metadata)Pointer metadata

Pointers and references can be thought of as having two parts: a data address and some extra “pointer metadata”.

Pointers to [statically-sized types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) and `extern` types are
“narrow”: their pointer metadata is `()`.

Pointers to [dynamically-sized types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/dynamically-sized-types.html) are “wide”: they have pointer
metadata with a non-zero size. There are four classes of dynamically-sized
types currently available:

- `str`s have- `usize`pointer metadata equal to the length of the string slice in bytes.
- Slices like `[i32]`have`usize`pointer metadata equal to the length of the slice in items.
- Trait objects like `dyn SomeTrait`have`DynMetadata`
- Structs with a trailing DST have the same metadata as the trailing DST.

In the future, Rust may add new kinds of types which have different pointer metadata.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

The associated `Metadata` type must be the pointer metadata type for the
implementing type.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

---

# to_raw_parts in ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ptr_meta/0.3.1/ptr_meta/fn.to_raw_parts.html

`pub const fn to_raw_parts<T: `[Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)>(
    ptr: [*const T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html),
) -> ([*const ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), <T as [Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html)>::[Metadata](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html#associatedtype.Metadata))## Expand description

Returns the data address and metadata of the given pointer.

`*mut T`, `&T`, and `&mut T` can all be passed directly to this function as
they implicitly coerce to `*const T`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
let (data_address, metadata) = ptr_meta::to_raw_parts("foo");
assert_ne!(data_address, core::ptr::null());
assert_eq!(metadata, 3);
```

---

# metadata in ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ptr_meta/0.3.1/ptr_meta/fn.metadata.html

## Expand description

Returns the metadata of the given pointer.

`*mut T`, `&T`, and `&mut T` can all be passed directly to this function as
they implicitly coerce to `*const T`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// String slices have pointer metadata equal to their size in bytes
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata("foo"), 3_usize);
```

# DynMetadata in ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ptr_meta/0.3.1/ptr_meta/struct.DynMetadata.html

`pub struct DynMetadata<Dyn: ?`[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

The metadata for a trait object.

This struct wraps a pointer to a vtable (virtual method table) which contains all of the necessary information to manipulate the concrete type stored inside of the trait object:

- The size and alignment of the concrete type
- A function pointer to the type’s `drop_in_place`impl
- Function pointers for each method in the concrete type’s trait implementation

Providing a type argument that is not a `dyn` trait object is possible, but
does not correspond with a meaningful type.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/ptr_meta/lib.rs.html#419-425)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Ord-for-DynMetadata%3CDyn%3E)### impl<Dyn: ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)> [Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html) for [DynMetadata](https://docs.rs/struct.DynMetadata.html)<Dyn>

# ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ptr_meta/latest/ptr_meta/

## Expand description

A radioactive stabilization of the [ ptr_meta RFC](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2580-ptr-meta.html).

This crate provides the [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) trait,

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)

`from_raw_parts`[functions, and proc macros for deriving](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)

`to_raw_parts``Pointee` for
structs and implementing `Pointee` for trait objects.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Raw pointers can be decomposed into the data address and metadata components
with [ to_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)

`to_raw_parts_mut`Alternatively, metadata alone can be extracted with the [ metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
function. Although

[accepts pointers, references can be passed and will be implicitly coerced.](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)

`metadata`A pointer can be created from its address and metadata with
[ from_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)

`from_raw_parts_mut`[§](https://docs.rs#provided-impls)Provided impls

`ptr_meta` provides inherent implementations for many builtin types:

- All `Sized``Pointee`
- `slice`,- `str`, and- `CStr`
- `OsStr`(requires- `std`)
- `dyn Any`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`
- `dyn Error`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`

[§](https://docs.rs#structs-with-trailing-dsts)Structs with trailing DSTs

You can derive [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) for structs with trailing DSTs:

```
use ptr_meta::Pointee;
#[derive(Pointee)]
struct Block<H, T> {
    header: H,
    elements: [T],
}
```
Note that the last field is required to be a DST. Structs with a generic
type as the last field may have conflicting blanket implementations, as the
generic type may be `Sized`. A collection of specific implementations may be
required in these cases, with the generic parameter set (for example) a
slice, `str`, or specific trait object.

[§](https://docs.rs#trait-objects)Trait objects

You can generate [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) implementations for trait objects:

```
use ptr_meta::pointee;
// Generates Pointee for dyn Stringy
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Stringy {
    fn as_string(&self) -> String;
}
```
Note that this will not produce implementations for `Trait + Send + Sync`.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `derive`: Re-exports the macros from- `ptr_meta_derive`. Enabled by default.
- `std`: Enables additional impls for- `std`types. Enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Get the associated metadata for pointers
let str = "hello world";
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(str), str.len());
let slice = &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5] as &[i32];
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(slice), slice.len());
// Make your own wide pointers from data pointers and metadata
let bytes = [b'h', b'e', b'l', b'l', b'o'];
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<str>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
println!("{} world!", unsafe { &*ptr }); // prints "hello world!"
// Derive Pointee on your own types
#[derive(ptr_meta::Pointee)]
#[repr(transparent)]
struct CoolStr {
    inner: str,
}
impl CoolStr {
    fn print_cool(&self) {
        println!("😎 {} 😎", &self.inner);
    }
}
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<CoolStr>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
let cool = unsafe { &*ptr };
cool.print_cool(); // prints "😎 hello 😎"
// Implement Pointee for trait objects
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Printable {
    fn print(&self);
}
impl Printable for i32 {
    fn print(&self) {
        println!("i32: {self}");
    }
}
let i32_vtable = ptr_meta::metadata(&0i32 as &dyn Printable);
let one_hundred = 100i32;
let printable = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<dyn Printable>(
    (&one_hundred as *const i32).cast(),
    i32_vtable,
);
unsafe {
    (*printable).print(); // prints "i32: 100"
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [DynMetadata](https://docs.rs/struct.DynMetadata.html)
- The metadata for a trait object.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html)
- A trait which associates pointer metadata with a pointee type.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns a raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns a mutable raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
- Returns the metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns the data address and metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns the mutable data address and metadata of the given pointer.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [pointee](https://docs.rs/attr.pointee.html)- `derive`
- Generates a `Pointee`implementation for trait object of the labeled trait.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/derive.Pointee.html)- `derive`
- Derives `Pointee`for the labeled struct which has a trailing DST.

---

# ptr_meta 0.3.0-alpha.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ptr_meta/0.3.0-alpha.2

A radioactive stabilization of the [ ptr_meta RFC](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2580-ptr-meta.html).

## Usage

### Sized types

All `Sized` types have `Pointee` implemented for them with a blanket
implementation. You do not need to derive `Pointee` for these types.

`slice`s and `str`s

These core types have implementations provided.

`CStr` and `OsStr`

These std types have implementations provided when the `std` feature is
enabled.

`dyn Any` and `dyn Error`

These trait objects have implementations provided.

### Structs with a DST as its last field

You can derive `Pointee` for structs with a trailing DST:

```
use Pointee;
```
Note that this will only work when the last field is guaranteed to be a DST.
Structs with a generic last field may have a conflicting blanket impl since
the generic type may be `Sized`. In these cases, a collection of specific
implementations may be required with the generic parameter set to a slice,
`str`, or specific trait object.

### Trait objects

You can generate a `Pointee` implementation for trait objects:

```
use pointee;
// Generates Pointee for dyn Stringy
```

# ptr_meta 0.2.0 - Docs.rs

A radioactive stabilization of the [ ptr_meta RFC](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2580-ptr-meta.html).

# Usage

## Sized types

All `Sized` types have `Pointee` implemented for them with a blanket implementation. You do not
need to derive `Pointee` for these types.

`slice`s and `str`s

These core types have implementations built in.

`dyn Any`

The trait object for this standard library type comes with an implementation built in.

## Structs with a DST as its last field

You can derive `Pointee` for structs with a trailing DST:

```
use Pointee;
```
Note that this will only work when the last field is guaranteed to be a DST. Structs with a
generic last field may have a conflicting blanket impl since the generic type may be `Sized`. In
these cases, a collection of specific implementations may be required with the generic parameter
set to a slice, `str`, or specific trait object.

## Trait objects

You can generate a `Pointee` implementation for trait objects:

```
use pointee;
// Generates Pointee for dyn Stringy
```

# ptr_meta 0.1.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ptr_meta/0.1.4

# ptr_meta

A radioactive stabilization of the [ ptr_meta RFC](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2580-ptr-meta.html).

## Usage

### Sized types

Sized types already have `Pointee` implemented for them, so most of the time you won't have to worry
about them. However, trying to derive `Pointee` for a struct that may or may not have a DST as its
last field will cause an implementation conflict with the automatic sized implementation.

`slice`s and `str`s

These core types have implementations built in.

### Structs with a DST as its last field

You can derive `Pointee` for last-field DSTs:

```
use Pointee;
```
### Trait objects

You can generate a `Pointee` for trait objects:

```
use pointee;
// Generates Pointee for dyn Stringy
```

---

# ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ptr_meta

## Expand description

A radioactive stabilization of the [ ptr_meta RFC](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2580-ptr-meta.html).

This crate provides the [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) trait,

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)

`from_raw_parts`[functions, and proc macros for deriving](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)

`to_raw_parts``Pointee` for
structs and implementing `Pointee` for trait objects.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

with [ to_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)

`to_raw_parts_mut`Alternatively, metadata alone can be extracted with the [ metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)

[accepts pointers, references can be passed and will be implicitly coerced.](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)

`metadata`A pointer can be created from its address and metadata with
[ from_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)

`from_raw_parts_mut`[§](https://docs.rs#provided-impls)Provided impls

    header: H,

[§](https://docs.rs#trait-objects)Trait objects

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Get the associated metadata for pointers
let str = "hello world";
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(str), str.len());
let slice = &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5] as &[i32];
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(slice), slice.len());

    inner: str,
}
impl CoolStr {
    fn print_cool(&self) {
        println!("😎 {} 😎", &self.inner);
    }
}
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<CoolStr>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
let cool = unsafe { &*ptr };
cool.print_cool(); // prints "😎 hello 😎"
// Implement Pointee for trait objects
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Printable {
    fn print(&self);
}
impl Printable for i32 {
    fn print(&self) {
        println!("i32: {self}");
    }
}
let i32_vtable = ptr_meta::metadata(&0i32 as &dyn Printable);
let one_hundred = 100i32;
let printable = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<dyn Printable>(
    (&one_hundred as *const i32).cast(),
    i32_vtable,
);
unsafe {
    (*printable).print(); // prints "i32: 100"
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [DynMetadata](https://docs.rs/struct.DynMetadata.html)
- The metadata for a trait object.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html)
- A trait which associates pointer metadata with a pointee type.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns a raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns a mutable raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
- Returns the metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns the data address and metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns the mutable data address and metadata of the given pointer.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [pointee](https://docs.rs/attr.pointee.html)- `derive`
- Generates a `Pointee`implementation for trait object of the labeled trait.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/derive.Pointee.html)- `derive`
- Derives `Pointee`for the labeled struct which has a trailing DST.

// Get the associated metadata for pointers
