# proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1/

## Expand description

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler’s [ proc_macro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/index.html)
crate. This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
#[proc_macro_derive(MyDerive)]
pub fn my_derive(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    let input = proc_macro2::TokenStream::from(input);
    let output: proc_macro2::TokenStream = {
        /* transform input */
    };
    proc_macro::TokenStream::from(output)
}
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you’ll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to
propagate parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable
compiler API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not
exposed by proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly
compiler, the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to
rustc. We will polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As
these are unstable APIs that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of
proc-macro2 may make breaking changes to them at any time.

`RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build`Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-safety)Thread-Safety

Most types in this crate are `!Sync` because the underlying compiler
types make use of thread-local memory, meaning they cannot be accessed from
a different thread.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

---

# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/^1/

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.

---

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Abi](https://docs.rs/struct.Abi.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The binary interface of a function: `extern "C"`.
- [Angle](https://docs.rs/struct.AngleBracketedGenericArguments.html)- Bracketed - Generic - Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed arguments of a path segment: the `<K, V>`in`HashMap<K, V>`.
- [Arm](https://docs.rs/struct.Arm.html)- `full`
- One arm of a `match`expression:`0..=10 => { return true; }`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocConst.html)- Const - `derive`or- `full`
- An equality constraint on an associated constant: the `PANIC = false`in`Trait<PANIC = false>`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- A binding (equality constraint) on an associated type: the `Item = u8`in`Iterator<Item = u8>`.
- [Attribute](https://docs.rs/struct.Attribute.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An attribute, like `#[repr(transparent)]`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareFnArg.html)- FnArg - `derive`or- `full`
- An argument in a function type: the `usize`in`fn(usize) -> bool`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareVariadic.html)- Variadic - `derive`or- `full`
- The variadic argument of a function pointer like `fn(usize, ...)`.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.Block.html)- `full`
- A braced block containing Rust statements.
- [Bound](https://docs.rs/struct.BoundLifetimes.html)- Lifetimes - `derive`or- `full`
- A set of bound lifetimes: `for<'a, 'b, 'c>`.
- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A const generic parameter: `const LENGTH: usize`.
- [Constraint](https://docs.rs/struct.Constraint.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An associated type bound: `Iterator<Item: Display>`.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataEnum.html)- Enum - `derive`
- An enum input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataStruct.html)- Struct - `derive`
- A struct input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataUnion.html)- Union - `derive`
- An untagged union input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Derive](https://docs.rs/struct.DeriveInput.html)- Input - `derive`
- Data structure sent to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error returned when a Syn parser cannot parse the input tokens.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprArray.html)- Array - `full`
- A slice literal expression: `[a, b, c, d]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAssign.html)- Assign - `full`
- An assignment expression: `a = compute()`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAsync.html)- Async - `full`
- An async block: `async { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAwait.html)- Await - `full`
- An await expression: `fut.await`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBinary.html)- Binary - `derive`or- `full`
- A binary operation: `a + b`,`a += b`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBlock.html)- Block - `full`
- A blocked scope: `{ ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBreak.html)- Break - `full`
- A `break`, with an optional label to break and an optional expression.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprCall.html)- Call - `derive`or- `full`
- A function call expression: `invoke(a, b)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprCast.html)- Cast - `derive`or- `full`
- A cast expression: `foo as f64`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprClosure.html)- Closure - `full`
- A closure expression: `|a, b| a + b`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprConst.html)- Const - `full`
- A const block: `const { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprContinue.html)- Continue - `full`
- A `continue`, with an optional label.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprField.html)- Field - `derive`or- `full`
- Access of a named struct field (`obj.k`) or unnamed tuple struct field (`obj.0`).
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprForLoop.html)- ForLoop - `full`
- A for loop: `for pat in expr { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprGroup.html)- Group - `full`
- An expression contained within invisible delimiters.
- [ExprIf](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprIf.html)- `full`
- An `if`expression with an optional`else`block:`if expr { ... } else { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprIndex.html)- Index - `derive`or- `full`
- A square bracketed indexing expression: `vector[2]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprInfer.html)- Infer - `full`
- The inferred value of a const generic argument, denoted `_`.
- [ExprLet](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLet.html)- `full`
- A `let`guard:`let Some(x) = opt`.
- [ExprLit](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLit.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A literal in place of an expression: `1`,`"foo"`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLoop.html)- Loop - `full`
- Conditionless loop: `loop { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMacro.html)- Macro - `derive`or- `full`
- A macro invocation expression: `format!("{}", q)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMatch.html)- Match - `full`
- A `match`expression:`match n { Some(n) => {}, None => {} }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMethodCall.html)- Method - Call - `derive`or- `full`
- A method call expression: `x.foo::<T>(a, b)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprParen.html)- Paren - `derive`or- `full`
- A parenthesized expression: `(a + b)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprPath.html)- Path - `derive`or- `full`
- A path like `core::mem::replace`possibly containing generic parameters and a qualified self-type.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprRange.html)- Range - `full`
- A range expression: `1..2`,`1..`,`..2`,`1..=2`,`..=2`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprRawAddr.html)- RawAddr - `full`
- Address-of operation: `&raw const place`or`&raw mut place`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprReference.html)- Reference - `derive`or- `full`
- A referencing operation: `&a`or`&mut a`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprRepeat.html)- Repeat - `full`
- An array literal constructed from one repeated element: `[0u8; N]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprReturn.html)- Return - `full`
- A `return`, with an optional value to be returned.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprStruct.html)- Struct - `derive`or- `full`
- A struct literal expression: `Point { x: 1, y: 1 }`.
- [ExprTry](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprTry.html)- `full`
- A try-expression: `expr?`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprTryBlock.html)- TryBlock - `full`
- A try block: `try { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprTuple.html)- Tuple - `full`
- A tuple expression: `(a, b, c, d)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprUnary.html)- Unary - `derive`or- `full`
- A unary operation: `!x`,`*x`,`-x`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprUnsafe.html)- Unsafe - `full`
- An unsafe block: `unsafe { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprWhile.html)- While - `full`
- A while loop: `while expr { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprYield.html)- Yield - `full`
- A yield expression: `yield expr`.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.Field.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A field of a struct or enum variant.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldPat.html)- Pat - `full`
- A single field in a struct pattern.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldValue.html)- Value - `derive`or- `full`
- A field-value pair in a struct literal.
- [Fields](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldsNamed.html)- Named - `derive`or- `full`
- Named fields of a struct or struct variant such as `Point { x: f64, y: f64 }`.
- [Fields](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldsUnnamed.html)- Unnamed - `derive`or- `full`
- Unnamed fields of a tuple struct or tuple variant such as `Some(T)`.
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.File.html)- `full`
- A complete file of Rust source code.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/struct.ForeignItemFn.html)- Item - Fn - `full`
- A foreign function in an `extern`block.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/struct.ForeignItemMacro.html)- Item - Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation within an extern block.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/struct.ForeignItemStatic.html)- Item - Static - `full`
- A foreign static item in an `extern`block:`static ext: u8`.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/struct.ForeignItemType.html)- Item - Type - `full`
- A foreign type in an `extern`block:`type void`.
- [Generics](https://docs.rs/struct.Generics.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Lifetimes and type parameters attached to a declaration of a function, enum, trait, etc.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/struct.ImplGenerics.html)- Generics - `printing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)

- [Impl](https://docs.rs/struct.ImplItemConst.html)- Item - Const - `full`

- [Impl](https://docs.rs/struct.ImplItemMacro.html)- Item - Macro - `full`

- [Impl](https://docs.rs/struct.ImplItemType.html)- Item - Type - `full`
- An associated type within an impl block.
- [Index](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The index of an unnamed tuple struct field.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemConst.html)- Const - `full`
- A constant item: `const MAX: u16 = 65535`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemEnum.html)- Enum - `full`
- An enum definition: `enum Foo<A, B> { A(A), B(B) }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemExternCrate.html)- Extern - Crate - `full`
- An `extern crate`item:`extern crate serde`.
- [ItemFn](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemFn.html)- `full`
- A free-standing function: `fn process(n: usize) -> Result<()> { ... }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemForeignMod.html)- Foreign - Mod - `full`
- A block of foreign items: `extern "C" { ... }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemImpl.html)- Impl - `full`
- An impl block providing trait or associated items: `impl<A> Trait for Data<A> { ... }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemMacro.html)- Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation, which includes `macro_rules!`definitions.
- [ItemMod](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemMod.html)- `full`
- A module or module declaration: `mod m`or`mod m { ... }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemStatic.html)- Static - `full`
- A static item: `static BIKE: Shed = Shed(42)`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemStruct.html)- Struct - `full`
- A struct definition: `struct Foo<A> { x: A }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemTrait.html)- Trait - `full`
- A trait definition: `pub trait Iterator { ... }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemTraitAlias.html)- Trait - Alias - `full`
- A trait alias: `pub trait SharableIterator = Iterator + Sync`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemType.html)- Type - `full`
- A type alias: `type Result<T> = core::result::Result<T, MyError>`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemUnion.html)- Union - `full`
- A union definition: `union Foo<A, B> { x: A, y: B }`.
- [ItemUse](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemUse.html)- `full`
- A use declaration: `use alloc::collections::HashMap`.
- [Label](https://docs.rs/struct.Label.html)- `full`
- A lifetime labeling a `for`,`while`, or`loop`.
- [Lifetime](https://docs.rs/struct.Lifetime.html)
- A Rust lifetime: `'a`.
- [Lifetime](https://docs.rs/struct.LifetimeParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A lifetime definition: `'a: 'b + 'c + 'd`.
- [LitBool](https://docs.rs/struct.LitBool.html)
- A boolean literal: `true`or`false`.
- [LitByte](https://docs.rs/struct.LitByte.html)
- A byte literal: `b'f'`.
- [LitByte](https://docs.rs/struct.LitByteStr.html)- Str
- A byte string literal: `b"foo"`.

- A nul-terminated C-string literal: `c"foo"`.
- [LitChar](https://docs.rs/struct.LitChar.html)
- A character literal: `'a'`.
- [LitFloat](https://docs.rs/struct.LitFloat.html)
- A floating point literal: `1f64`or`1.0e10f64`.
- [LitInt](https://docs.rs/struct.LitInt.html)
- An integer literal: `1`or`1u16`.
- [LitStr](https://docs.rs/struct.LitStr.html)
- A UTF-8 string literal: `"foo"`.
- [Local](https://docs.rs/struct.Local.html)- `full`
- A local `let`binding:`let x: u64 = s.parse()?;`.
- [Local](https://docs.rs/struct.LocalInit.html)- Init - `full`
- The expression assigned in a local `let`binding, including optional diverging`else`block.
- [Macro](https://docs.rs/struct.Macro.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A macro invocation: `println!("{}", mac)`.
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/struct.MetaList.html)- List - `derive`or- `full`
- A structured list within an attribute, like `derive(Copy, Clone)`.
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/struct.MetaNameValue.html)- Name - Value - `derive`or- `full`

- [Parenthesized](https://docs.rs/struct.ParenthesizedGenericArguments.html)- Generic - Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Arguments of a function path segment: the `(A, B) -> C`in`Fn(A,B) -> C`.

- [PatIdent](https://docs.rs/struct.PatIdent.html)- `full`

- [PatLit](https://docs.rs/struct.PatLit.html)- `full`

- [PatMacro](https://docs.rs/struct.PatMacro.html)- `full`

- [PatOr](https://docs.rs/struct.PatOr.html)- `full`

- [PatParen](https://docs.rs/struct.PatParen.html)- `full`

- [PatSlice](https://docs.rs/struct.PatSlice.html)- `full`

- [PatStruct](https://docs.rs/struct.PatStruct.html)- `full`

- [PatTuple](https://docs.rs/struct.PatTuple.html)- `full`

- [PatTuple](https://docs.rs/struct.PatTupleStruct.html)- Struct - `full`

- [PatType](https://docs.rs/struct.PatType.html)- `full`

- [PatWild](https://docs.rs/struct.PatWild.html)- `full`

- [Path](https://docs.rs/struct.Path.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A path at which a named item is exported (e.g. `alloc::collections::HashMap`).
- [Path](https://docs.rs/struct.PathSegment.html)- Segment - `derive`or- `full`

- [Precise](https://docs.rs/struct.PreciseCapture.html)- Capture - `full`

- [Predicate](https://docs.rs/struct.PredicateLifetime.html)- Lifetime - `derive`or- `full`
- A lifetime predicate in a `where`clause:`'a: 'b + 'c`.
- [Predicate](https://docs.rs/struct.PredicateType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`

- [QSelf](https://docs.rs/struct.QSelf.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The explicit Self type in a qualified path: the `T`in`<T as Display>::fmt`.
- [Receiver](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)- `full`
- The `self`argument of an associated method.
- [Signature](https://docs.rs/struct.Signature.html)- `full`
- A function signature in a trait or implementation: `unsafe fn initialize(&self)`.
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/struct.StmtMacro.html)- Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation in statement position.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitBound.html)- Bound - `derive`or- `full`
- A trait used as a bound on a type parameter.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemConst.html)- Item - Const - `full`
- An associated constant within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemFn.html)- Item - Fn - `full`
- An associated function within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemMacro.html)- Item - Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemType.html)- Item - Type - `full`
- An associated type within the definition of a trait.
- [Turbofish](https://docs.rs/struct.Turbofish.html)- `printing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Returned by `TypeGenerics::as_turbofish`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeArray.html)- Array - `derive`or- `full`
- A fixed size array type: `[T; n]`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeBareFn.html)- Bare - Fn - `derive`or- `full`
- A bare function type: `fn(usize) -> bool`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeGenerics.html)- Generics - `printing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Returned by `Generics::split_for_impl`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeGroup.html)- Group - `derive`or- `full`
- A type contained within invisible delimiters.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeImplTrait.html)- Impl - Trait - `derive`or- `full`
- An `impl Bound1 + Bound2 + Bound3`type where`Bound`is a trait or a lifetime.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeInfer.html)- Infer - `derive`or- `full`
- Indication that a type should be inferred by the compiler: `_`.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeMacro.html)- Macro - `derive`or- `full`
- A macro in the type position.

# ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ptr_meta/latest/target-redirect/ptr_meta/index.html

## Expand description

A radioactive stabilization of the [ ptr_meta RFC](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2580-ptr-meta.html).

This crate provides the [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) trait,

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)

`from_raw_parts`[functions, and proc macros for deriving](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)

`to_raw_parts``Pointee` for
structs and implementing `Pointee` for trait objects.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Raw pointers can be decomposed into the data address and metadata components
with [ to_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)

`to_raw_parts_mut`Alternatively, metadata alone can be extracted with the [ metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
function. Although

[accepts pointers, references can be passed and will be implicitly coerced.](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)

`metadata`A pointer can be created from its address and metadata with
[ from_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)

`from_raw_parts_mut`[§](https://docs.rs#provided-impls)Provided impls

`ptr_meta` provides inherent implementations for many builtin types:

- All `Sized``Pointee`
- `slice`,- `str`, and- `CStr`
- `OsStr`(requires- `std`)
- `dyn Any`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`
- `dyn Error`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`

[§](https://docs.rs#structs-with-trailing-dsts)Structs with trailing DSTs

You can derive [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) for structs with trailing DSTs:

```
use ptr_meta::Pointee;
#[derive(Pointee)]
struct Block<H, T> {
    header: H,
    elements: [T],
}
```
Note that the last field is required to be a DST. Structs with a generic
type as the last field may have conflicting blanket implementations, as the
generic type may be `Sized`. A collection of specific implementations may be
required in these cases, with the generic parameter set (for example) a
slice, `str`, or specific trait object.

[§](https://docs.rs#trait-objects)Trait objects

You can generate [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) implementations for trait objects:

```
use ptr_meta::pointee;
// Generates Pointee for dyn Stringy
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Stringy {
    fn as_string(&self) -> String;
}
```
Note that this will not produce implementations for `Trait + Send + Sync`.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `derive`: Re-exports the macros from- `ptr_meta_derive`. Enabled by default.
- `std`: Enables additional impls for- `std`types. Enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Get the associated metadata for pointers
let str = "hello world";
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(str), str.len());
let slice = &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5] as &[i32];
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(slice), slice.len());
// Make your own wide pointers from data pointers and metadata
let bytes = [b'h', b'e', b'l', b'l', b'o'];
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<str>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
println!("{} world!", unsafe { &*ptr }); // prints "hello world!"
// Derive Pointee on your own types
#[derive(ptr_meta::Pointee)]
#[repr(transparent)]
struct CoolStr {
    inner: str,
}
impl CoolStr {
    fn print_cool(&self) {
        println!("😎 {} 😎", &self.inner);
    }
}
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<CoolStr>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
let cool = unsafe { &*ptr };
cool.print_cool(); // prints "😎 hello 😎"
// Implement Pointee for trait objects
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Printable {
    fn print(&self);
}
impl Printable for i32 {
    fn print(&self) {
        println!("i32: {self}");
    }
}
let i32_vtable = ptr_meta::metadata(&0i32 as &dyn Printable);
let one_hundred = 100i32;
let printable = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<dyn Printable>(
    (&one_hundred as *const i32).cast(),
    i32_vtable,
);
unsafe {
    (*printable).print(); // prints "i32: 100"
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [DynMetadata](https://docs.rs/struct.DynMetadata.html)
- The metadata for a trait object.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html)
- A trait which associates pointer metadata with a pointee type.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns a raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns a mutable raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
- Returns the metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns the data address and metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns the mutable data address and metadata of the given pointer.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [pointee](https://docs.rs/attr.pointee.html)- `derive`
- Generates a `Pointee`implementation for trait object of the labeled trait.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/derive.Pointee.html)- `derive`
- Derives `Pointee`for the labeled struct which has a trailing DST.

# ptr_meta/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! A radioactive stabilization of the [`ptr_meta` RFC][rfc].
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! This crate provides the [`Pointee`] trait, [`from_raw_parts`] and
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! [`to_raw_parts`] functions, and proc macros for deriving `Pointee` for
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! structs and implementing `Pointee` for trait objects.
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! [rfc]: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2580-ptr-meta.html
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! # Usage
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! Raw pointers can be decomposed into the data address and metadata components
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! with [`to_raw_parts`] or [`to_raw_parts_mut`].
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! Alternatively, metadata alone can be extracted with the [`metadata`]
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! function. Although [`metadata`] accepts pointers, references can be passed
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! and will be implicitly coerced.
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! A pointer can be created from its address and metadata with
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! [`from_raw_parts`] or [`from_raw_parts_mut`].
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! ## Provided impls
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! `ptr_meta` provides inherent implementations for many builtin types:
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! - All [`Sized`] types implement [`Pointee`] via a blanket implementation.
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! - `slice`, `str`, and `CStr`
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! - `OsStr` (requires `std`)
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! - `dyn Any`, optionally with `+ Send` and/or `+ Sync`
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! - `dyn Error`, optionally with `+ Send` and/or `+ Sync`
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! ## Structs with trailing DSTs
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! You can derive [`Pointee`] for structs with trailing DSTs:
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! ```
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! use ptr_meta::Pointee;
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! #[derive(Pointee)]
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! struct Block<H, T> {
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!     header: H,
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!     elements: [T],
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! }
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! ```
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! Note that the last field is required to be a DST. Structs with a generic
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! type as the last field may have conflicting blanket implementations, as the
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! generic type may be `Sized`. A collection of specific implementations may be
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! required in these cases, with the generic parameter set (for example) a
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! slice, `str`, or specific trait object.
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! ## Trait objects
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! You can generate [`Pointee`] implementations for trait objects:
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! ```
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! use ptr_meta::pointee;
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! // Generates Pointee for dyn Stringy
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! #[ptr_meta::pointee]
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! trait Stringy {
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!     fn as_string(&self) -> String;
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! }
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! ```
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!

[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!

[101](https://docs.rs#101)pub use ptr_meta_derive::{pointee, Pointee};
[102](https://docs.rs#102)
[103](https://docs.rs#103)/// A trait which associates pointer metadata with a pointee type.
[104](https://docs.rs#104)///
[105](https://docs.rs#105)/// # Pointer metadata
[106](https://docs.rs#106)///
[107](https://docs.rs#107)/// Pointers and references can be thought of as having two parts: a data
[108](https://docs.rs#108)/// address and some extra "pointer metadata".
[109](https://docs.rs#109)///
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// Pointers to [statically-sized types](`Sized`) and `extern` types are
[111](https://docs.rs#111)/// "narrow": their pointer metadata is `()`.
[112](https://docs.rs#112)///
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// Pointers to [dynamically-sized types][dst] are "wide": they have pointer
[114](https://docs.rs#114)/// metadata with a non-zero size. There are four classes of dynamically-sized
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// types currently available:
[116](https://docs.rs#116)///
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// * `str`s have `usize` pointer metadata equal to the length of the string
[118](https://docs.rs#118)///   slice in bytes.
[119](https://docs.rs#119)/// * Slices like `[i32]` have `usize` pointer metadata equal to the length of
[120](https://docs.rs#120)///   the slice in items.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)/// * Trait objects like `dyn SomeTrait` have [`DynMetadata`] pointer metadata,
[122](https://docs.rs#122)///   which point to the trait objects' virtual method tables.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)/// * Structs with a trailing DST have the same metadata as the trailing DST.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)///
[125](https://docs.rs#125)/// In the future, Rust may add new kinds of types which have different pointer
[126](https://docs.rs#126)/// metadata.
[127](https://docs.rs#127)///
[128](https://docs.rs#128)/// [dst]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/dynamically-sized-types.html
[129](https://docs.rs#129)///
[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// # Safety
[131](https://docs.rs#131)///
[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// The associated `Metadata` type must be the pointer metadata type for the
[133](https://docs.rs#133)/// implementing type.
[134](https://docs.rs#134)pub unsafe trait Pointee {
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    /// The metadata type for pointers and references to this type.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)    type Metadata: Copy + Send + Sync + Ord + Hash + Unpin;
[137](https://docs.rs#137)}
[138](https://docs.rs#138)
[139](https://docs.rs#139)// SAFETY: Pointers to `Sized` types have no metadata (i.e. their metadata is
[140](https://docs.rs#140)// the unit type `()`).
[141](https://docs.rs#141)unsafe impl<T> Pointee for T {
[142](https://docs.rs#142)    type Metadata = ();
[143](https://docs.rs#143)}
[144](https://docs.rs#144)
[145](https://docs.rs#145)// SAFETY: Pointers to slices have a `usize` representing the length of the
[146](https://docs.rs#146)// slice in elements as their metadata.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)unsafe impl<T> Pointee for [T] {
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    type Metadata = usize;
[149](https://docs.rs#149)}
[150](https://docs.rs#150)
[151](https://docs.rs#151)// SAFETY: String slice pointers have a `usize` representing the length of the
[152](https://docs.rs#152)// string slice in bytes as their metadata.
[153](https://docs.rs#153)unsafe impl Pointee for str {
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    type Metadata = usize;
[155](https://docs.rs#155)}
[156](https://docs.rs#156)
[157](https://docs.rs#157)// SAFETY: `CStr` pointers have a `usize` representing the length of the
[158](https://docs.rs#158)// C-string slice in bytes (nul included) as their metadata.
[159](https://docs.rs#159)unsafe impl Pointee for CStr {
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    type Metadata = usize;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)}
[162](https://docs.rs#162)
[163](https://docs.rs#163)#[cfg(feature = "std")]
[164](https://docs.rs#164)// SAFETY: `OsStr` pointers have a `usize` representing the length of the
[165](https://docs.rs#165)// string in bytes as their metadata.
[166](https://docs.rs#166)unsafe impl Pointee for std::ffi::OsStr {
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    type Metadata = usize;
[168](https://docs.rs#168)}
[169](https://docs.rs#169)
[170](https://docs.rs#170)/// Returns the metadata of the given pointer.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)///
[172](https://docs.rs#172)/// `*mut T`, `&T`, and `&mut T` can all be passed directly to this function as
[173](https://docs.rs#173)/// they implicitly coerce to `*const T`.
[174](https://docs.rs#174)///
[175](https://docs.rs#175)/// # Example
[176](https://docs.rs#176)///
[177](https://docs.rs#177)/// ```
[178](https://docs.rs#178)/// // String slices have pointer metadata equal to their size in bytes
[179](https://docs.rs#179)/// assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata("foo"), 3_usize);
[180](https://docs.rs#180)/// ```
[181](https://docs.rs#181)#[inline]
[182](https://docs.rs#182)pub const fn metadata<T: Pointee + ?Sized>(
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    ptr: *const T,
[184](https://docs.rs#184)) -> <T as Pointee>::Metadata {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    // SAFETY: Accessing the value from the `PtrRepr` union is safe since
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    // *const T and PtrComponents<T> have the same memory layouts. Only std can
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    // make this guarantee.
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    unsafe { PtrRepr { const_ptr: ptr }.components.metadata }
[189](https://docs.rs#189)}
[190](https://docs.rs#190)
[191](https://docs.rs#191)/// Returns the data address and metadata of the given pointer.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)///
[193](https://docs.rs#193)/// `*mut T`, `&T`, and `&mut T` can all be passed directly to this function as
[194](https://docs.rs#194)/// they implicitly coerce to `*const T`.
[195](https://docs.rs#195)///
[196](https://docs.rs#196)/// # Example
[197](https://docs.rs#197)///
[198](https://docs.rs#198)/// ```
[199](https://docs.rs#199)/// let (data_address, metadata) = ptr_meta::to_raw_parts("foo");
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// assert_ne!(data_address, core::ptr::null());
[201](https://docs.rs#201)/// assert_eq!(metadata, 3);
[202](https://docs.rs#202)/// ```
[203](https://docs.rs#203)#[inline]
[204](https://docs.rs#204)pub const fn to_raw_parts<T: Pointee + ?Sized>(
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    ptr: *const T,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)) -> (*const (), <T as Pointee>::Metadata) {
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    (ptr as *const (), metadata(ptr))
[208](https://docs.rs#208)}
[209](https://docs.rs#209)
[210](https://docs.rs#210)/// Returns the mutable data address and metadata of the given pointer.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)///
[212](https://docs.rs#212)/// See [`to_raw_parts`] for more details.
[213](https://docs.rs#213)#[inline]
[214](https://docs.rs#214)pub const fn to_raw_parts_mut<T: Pointee + ?Sized>(
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    ptr: *mut T,
[216](https://docs.rs#216)) -> (*mut (), <T as Pointee>::Metadata) {
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    (ptr as *mut (), metadata(ptr))
[218](https://docs.rs#218)}
[219](https://docs.rs#219)
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// Returns a raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
[221](https://docs.rs#221)///
[222](https://docs.rs#222)/// This function is safe, but the returned pointer is not necessarily safe to
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// dereference. For slices, see the documentation of [`slice::from_raw_parts`]
[224](https://docs.rs#224)/// for safety requirements. For trait objects, the metadata must come from a
[225](https://docs.rs#225)/// a trait object with the same underlying type.
[226](https://docs.rs#226)///
[227](https://docs.rs#227)/// [`slice::from_raw_parts`]: core::slice::from_raw_parts
[228](https://docs.rs#228)#[inline]
[229](https://docs.rs#229)pub const fn from_raw_parts<T: Pointee + ?Sized>(
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    data_address: *const (),
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    metadata: <T as Pointee>::Metadata,
[232](https://docs.rs#232)) -> *const T {
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    // SAFETY: Accessing the value from the `PtrRepr` union is safe since
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    // *const T and PtrComponents<T> have the same memory layouts. Only std can
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    // make this guarantee.
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    unsafe {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        PtrRepr {
[238](https://docs.rs#238)            components: PtrComponents {
[239](https://docs.rs#239)                data_address,
[240](https://docs.rs#240)                metadata,
[241](https://docs.rs#241)            },
[242](https://docs.rs#242)        }
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        .const_ptr
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)}
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// Returns a mutable raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)///
[249](https://docs.rs#249)/// See [`from_raw_parts`] for more details.
[250](https://docs.rs#250)#[inline]
[251](https://docs.rs#251)pub const fn from_raw_parts_mut<T: Pointee + ?Sized>(
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    data_address: *mut (),
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    metadata: <T as Pointee>::Metadata,
[254](https://docs.rs#254)) -> *mut T {
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    // SAFETY: Accessing the value from the `PtrRepr` union is safe since
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    // *const T and PtrComponents<T> have the same memory layouts. Only std can
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    // make this guarantee.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    unsafe {
[259](https://docs.rs#259)        PtrRepr {
[260](https://docs.rs#260)            components: PtrComponents {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)                data_address,
[262](https://docs.rs#262)                metadata,
[263](https://docs.rs#263)            },
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        }
[265](https://docs.rs#265)        .mut_ptr
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    }
[267](https://docs.rs#267)}
[268](https://docs.rs#268)
[269](https://docs.rs#269)#[repr(C)]
[270](https://docs.rs#270)union PtrRepr<T: Pointee + ?Sized> {
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    const_ptr: *const T,
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    mut_ptr: *mut T,
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    components: PtrComponents<T>,
[274](https://docs.rs#274)}
[275](https://docs.rs#275)
[276](https://docs.rs#276)#[repr(C)]
[277](https://docs.rs#277)struct PtrComponents<T: Pointee + ?Sized> {
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    data_address: *const (),
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    metadata: <T as Pointee>::Metadata,
[280](https://docs.rs#280)}
[281](https://docs.rs#281)
[282](https://docs.rs#282)// Manual impl needed to avoid `T: Copy` bound.
[283](https://docs.rs#283)impl<T: Pointee + ?Sized> Copy for PtrComponents<T> {}
[284](https://docs.rs#284)
[285](https://docs.rs#285)// Manual impl needed to avoid `T: Clone` bound.
[286](https://docs.rs#286)impl<T: Pointee + ?Sized> Clone for PtrComponents<T> {
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
[288](https://docs.rs#288)        *self
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    }
[290](https://docs.rs#290)}
[291](https://docs.rs#291)
[292](https://docs.rs#292)/// The metadata for a trait object.
[293](https://docs.rs#293)///
[294](https://docs.rs#294)/// This struct wraps a pointer to a vtable (virtual method table) which
[295](https://docs.rs#295)/// contains all of the necessary information to manipulate the concrete type
[296](https://docs.rs#296)/// stored inside of the trait object:
[297](https://docs.rs#297)///
[298](https://docs.rs#298)/// * The size and alignment of the concrete type
[299](https://docs.rs#299)/// * A function pointer to the type's `drop_in_place` impl
[300](https://docs.rs#300)/// * Function pointers for each method in the concrete type's trait
[301](https://docs.rs#301)///   implementation
[302](https://docs.rs#302)///
[303](https://docs.rs#303)/// Providing a type argument that is not a `dyn` trait object is possible, but
[304](https://docs.rs#304)/// does not correspond with a meaningful type.
[305](https://docs.rs#305)pub struct DynMetadata<Dyn: ?Sized> {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    vtable_ptr: &'static VTable,
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<Dyn>,
[308](https://docs.rs#308)}
[309](https://docs.rs#309)
[310](https://docs.rs#310)// Extern types are not stable, so we substitute a ZST. This is not a perfect
[311](https://docs.rs#311)// substitute but it's not exposed anywhere so it's close enough.
[312](https://docs.rs#312)struct VTable;
[313](https://docs.rs#313)
[314](https://docs.rs#314)impl<Dyn: ?Sized> DynMetadata<Dyn> {
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    /// Returns the size of the type associated with this metadata.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    #[inline]
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    pub fn size_of(self) -> usize {
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        #[cfg(miri)]
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        {
[320](https://docs.rs#320)            // Note that "size stored in vtable" is *not* the same as "result of
[321](https://docs.rs#321)            // size_of_val_raw". Consider a reference like `&(i32,
[322](https://docs.rs#322)            // dyn Send)`: the vtable will only store the size of the
[323](https://docs.rs#323)            // `Send` part!
[324](https://docs.rs#324)            // SAFETY: DynMetadata always contains a valid vtable pointer
[325](https://docs.rs#325)            return unsafe {
[326](https://docs.rs#326)                core::intrinsics::vtable_size(
[327](https://docs.rs#327)                    self.vtable_ptr as *const VTable as *const (),
[328](https://docs.rs#328)                )
[329](https://docs.rs#329)            };
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        }
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        #[cfg(not(miri))]
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)            // SAFETY: This happens to be true. It may not always be true. The
[334](https://docs.rs#334)            // location of the size for vtables is based on the implementation
[335](https://docs.rs#335)            // of the vtable_size intrinsic.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)            unsafe {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)                (self.vtable_ptr as *const VTable as *const usize)
[338](https://docs.rs#338)                    .add(1)
[339](https://docs.rs#339)                    .read()
[340](https://docs.rs#340)            }
[341](https://docs.rs#341)        }
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    }
[343](https://docs.rs#343)
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    /// Returns the alignment of the type associated with this metadata.
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    #[inline]
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    pub fn align_of(self) -> usize {
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        #[cfg(miri)]
[348](https://docs.rs#348)        {
[349](https://docs.rs#349)            // SAFETY: DynMetadata always contains a valid vtable pointer
[350](https://docs.rs#350)            return unsafe {
[351](https://docs.rs#351)                core::intrinsics::vtable_align(
[352](https://docs.rs#352)                    self.vtable_ptr as *const VTable as *const (),
[353](https://docs.rs#353)                )
[354](https://docs.rs#354)            };
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        }
[356](https://docs.rs#356)        #[cfg(not(miri))]
[357](https://docs.rs#357)        {
[358](https://docs.rs#358)            // SAFETY: This happens to be true. It may not always be true. The
[359](https://docs.rs#359)            // location of the alignment for vtables is based on the
[360](https://docs.rs#360)            // implementation of the vtable_align intrinsic.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)            unsafe {
[362](https://docs.rs#362)                (self.vtable_ptr as *const VTable as *const usize)
[363](https://docs.rs#363)                    .add(2)
[364](https://docs.rs#364)                    .read()
[365](https://docs.rs#365)            }
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        }
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    }
[368](https://docs.rs#368)
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// Returns the layout of the type associated with this metadata.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    #[inline]
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    pub fn layout(self) -> core::alloc::Layout {
[372](https://docs.rs#372)        // SAFETY: the compiler emitted this vtable for a concrete Rust type
[373](https://docs.rs#373)        // which is known to have a valid layout. Same rationale as in
[374](https://docs.rs#374)        // `Layout::for_value`.
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        unsafe {
[376](https://docs.rs#376)            core::alloc::Layout::from_size_align_unchecked(
[377](https://docs.rs#377)                self.size_of(),
[378](https://docs.rs#378)                self.align_of(),
[379](https://docs.rs#379)            )
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        }
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    }
[382](https://docs.rs#382)}
[383](https://docs.rs#383)
[384](https://docs.rs#384)// SAFETY: References to trait object vtables are guaranteed to be `Send`.
[385](https://docs.rs#385)unsafe impl<Dyn: ?Sized> Send for DynMetadata<Dyn> {}
[386](https://docs.rs#386)// SAFETY: References to trait object vtables are guaranteed to be `Sync`.
[387](https://docs.rs#387)unsafe impl<Dyn: ?Sized> Sync for DynMetadata<Dyn> {}
[388](https://docs.rs#388)
[389](https://docs.rs#389)impl<Dyn: ?Sized> fmt::Debug for DynMetadata<Dyn> {
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
[391](https://docs.rs#391)        f.debug_tuple("DynMetadata")
[392](https://docs.rs#392)            .field(&(self.vtable_ptr as *const VTable))
[393](https://docs.rs#393)            .finish()
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    }
[395](https://docs.rs#395)}
[396](https://docs.rs#396)
[397](https://docs.rs#397)// Manual impls needed to avoid `Dyn: $Trait` bounds.
[398](https://docs.rs#398)
[399](https://docs.rs#399)impl<Dyn: ?Sized> Unpin for DynMetadata<Dyn> {}
[400](https://docs.rs#400)
[401](https://docs.rs#401)impl<Dyn: ?Sized> Copy for DynMetadata<Dyn> {}
[402](https://docs.rs#402)
[403](https://docs.rs#403)impl<Dyn: ?Sized> Clone for DynMetadata<Dyn> {
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    #[inline]
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
[406](https://docs.rs#406)        *self
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    }
[408](https://docs.rs#408)}
[409](https://docs.rs#409)
[410](https://docs.rs#410)impl<Dyn: ?Sized> Eq for DynMetadata<Dyn> {}
[411](https://docs.rs#411)
[412](https://docs.rs#412)impl<Dyn: ?Sized> PartialEq for DynMetadata<Dyn> {
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    #[inline]
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    fn eq(&self, other: &Self) -> bool {
[415](https://docs.rs#415)        core::ptr::eq::<VTable>(self.vtable_ptr, other.vtable_ptr)
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    }
[417](https://docs.rs#417)}
[418](https://docs.rs#418)
[419](https://docs.rs#419)impl<Dyn: ?Sized> Ord for DynMetadata<Dyn> {
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    #[inline]
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    fn cmp(&self, other: &Self) -> core::cmp::Ordering {
[422](https://docs.rs#422)        (self.vtable_ptr as *const VTable)
[423](https://docs.rs#423)            .cmp(&(other.vtable_ptr as *const VTable))
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    }
[425](https://docs.rs#425)}
[426](https://docs.rs#426)
[427](https://docs.rs#427)impl<Dyn: ?Sized> PartialOrd for DynMetadata<Dyn> {
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    #[inline]
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    fn partial_cmp(&self, other: &Self) -> Option<core::cmp::Ordering> {
[430](https://docs.rs#430)        Some(self.cmp(other))
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    }
[432](https://docs.rs#432)}
[433](https://docs.rs#433)
[434](https://docs.rs#434)impl<Dyn: ?Sized> Hash for DynMetadata<Dyn> {
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    #[inline]
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    fn hash<H: Hasher>(&self, hasher: &mut H) {
[437](https://docs.rs#437)        core::ptr::hash::<VTable, _>(self.vtable_ptr, hasher)
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    }
[439](https://docs.rs#439)}
[440](https://docs.rs#440)
[441](https://docs.rs#441)#[cfg(test)]
[442](https://docs.rs#442)fn test_pointee<T: Pointee + ?Sized>(value: &T) {
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    let ptr = value as *const T;
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    let (raw, meta) = to_raw_parts(ptr);
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    let re_ptr = from_raw_parts::<T>(raw, meta);
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    assert_eq!(ptr, re_ptr);
[447](https://docs.rs#447)}
[448](https://docs.rs#448)
[449](https://docs.rs#449)#[cfg(test)]
[450](https://docs.rs#450)mod tests {
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    use super::test_pointee;
[452](https://docs.rs#452)
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    #[test]
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    fn sized_types() {
[455](https://docs.rs#455)        test_pointee(&());
[456](https://docs.rs#456)        test_pointee(&42);
[457](https://docs.rs#457)        test_pointee(&true);
[458](https://docs.rs#458)        test_pointee(&[1, 2, 3, 4]);
[459](https://docs.rs#459)
[460](https://docs.rs#460)        struct TestUnit;
[461](https://docs.rs#461)
[462](https://docs.rs#462)        test_pointee(&TestUnit);
[463](https://docs.rs#463)
[464](https://docs.rs#464)        #[allow(dead_code)]
[465](https://docs.rs#465)        struct TestStruct {
[466](https://docs.rs#466)            a: (),
[467](https://docs.rs#467)            b: i32,
[468](https://docs.rs#468)            c: bool,
[469](https://docs.rs#469)        }
[470](https://docs.rs#470)
[471](https://docs.rs#471)        test_pointee(&TestStruct {
[472](https://docs.rs#472)            a: (),
[473](https://docs.rs#473)            b: 42,
[474](https://docs.rs#474)            c: true,
[475](https://docs.rs#475)        });
[476](https://docs.rs#476)
[477](https://docs.rs#477)        #[allow(dead_code)]
[478](https://docs.rs#478)        struct TestTuple((), i32, bool);
[479](https://docs.rs#479)
[480](https://docs.rs#480)        test_pointee(&TestTuple((), 42, true));
[481](https://docs.rs#481)
[482](https://docs.rs#482)        struct TestGeneric<T>(T);
[483](https://docs.rs#483)
[484](https://docs.rs#484)        test_pointee(&TestGeneric(42));
[485](https://docs.rs#485)    }

[491](https://docs.rs#491)    }

[494](https://docs.rs#494)#[cfg(all(test, feature = "derive"))]
[495](https://docs.rs#495)mod derive_tests {
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    use core::any::Any;
[497](https://docs.rs#497)
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    use super::{test_pointee, Pointee};
[499](https://docs.rs#499)
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    #[test]
[501](https://docs.rs#501)    fn trait_objects() {
[502](https://docs.rs#502)        #[crate::pointee(crate)]
[503](https://docs.rs#503)        trait TestTrait {
[504](https://docs.rs#504)            #[allow(dead_code)]
[505](https://docs.rs#505)            fn foo(&self);
[506](https://docs.rs#506)        }
[507](https://docs.rs#507)
[508](https://docs.rs#508)        struct A;
[509](https://docs.rs#509)
[510](https://docs.rs#510)        impl TestTrait for A {
[511](https://docs.rs#511)            fn foo(&self) {}
[512](https://docs.rs#512)        }
[513](https://docs.rs#513)
[514](https://docs.rs#514)        let trait_object = &A as &dyn TestTrait;

# Pointee in ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ptr_meta/latest/target-redirect/ptr_meta/trait.Pointee.html

## Expand description

A trait which associates pointer metadata with a pointee type.

[§](https://docs.rs#pointer-metadata)Pointer metadata

Pointers and references can be thought of as having two parts: a data address and some extra “pointer metadata”.

Pointers to [statically-sized types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) and `extern` types are
“narrow”: their pointer metadata is `()`.

Pointers to [dynamically-sized types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/dynamically-sized-types.html) are “wide”: they have pointer
metadata with a non-zero size. There are four classes of dynamically-sized
types currently available:

- `str`s have- `usize`pointer metadata equal to the length of the string slice in bytes.
- Slices like `[i32]`have`usize`pointer metadata equal to the length of the slice in items.
- Trait objects like `dyn SomeTrait`have`DynMetadata`
- Structs with a trailing DST have the same metadata as the trailing DST.

In the future, Rust may add new kinds of types which have different pointer metadata.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

The associated `Metadata` type must be the pointer metadata type for the
implementing type.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

---

# to_raw_parts in ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ptr_meta/latest/target-redirect/ptr_meta/fn.to_raw_parts.html

`pub const fn to_raw_parts<T: `[Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)>(
    ptr: [*const T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html),
) -> ([*const ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), <T as [Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html)>::[Metadata](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html#associatedtype.Metadata))## Expand description

Returns the data address and metadata of the given pointer.

`*mut T`, `&T`, and `&mut T` can all be passed directly to this function as
they implicitly coerce to `*const T`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
let (data_address, metadata) = ptr_meta::to_raw_parts("foo");
assert_ne!(data_address, core::ptr::null());
assert_eq!(metadata, 3);
```

---

# to_raw_parts_mut in ptr_meta - Rust

    ptr: [*mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html),
) -> ([*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), <T as [Pointee](trait.Pointee.html)>::[Metadata](trait.Pointee.html#associatedtype.Metadata))

# metadata in ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ptr_meta/latest/target-redirect/ptr_meta/fn.metadata.html

## Expand description

Returns the metadata of the given pointer.

`*mut T`, `&T`, and `&mut T` can all be passed directly to this function as
they implicitly coerce to `*const T`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// String slices have pointer metadata equal to their size in bytes
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata("foo"), 3_usize);
```

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`
- `snapbox`
- `assert_cmd`- `assert_fs`

Documentation:

- Allows you to build the `Command`instance from your Cargo.toml at compile time.

- Allows you to pull the authors for the command from your Cargo.toml at

`"author1 lastname <author1@example.com>:author2 lastname <author2@example.com>"`

`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH_PKGVERSION_PRE`

- The abstract representation of a command line argument. Used to set all the options and relationships that define a valid argument for the program.
- [ArgGroup](https://docs.rs/struct.ArgGroup.html)

- Create a `Command`

- Converts an instance of `ArgMatches`

- Parse command-line arguments into `Self`.

- Parse a sub-command into a user-defined enum.

- Parse arguments into enums.

- Converts an instance of `ArgMatches`
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)
- Parse command-line arguments into `Self`.
- [Subcommand](https://docs.rs/trait.Subcommand.html)
- Parse a sub-command into a user-defined enum.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/trait.ValueEnum.html)- Enum
- Parse arguments into enums.
